title: 3D Printing
desc: Learn to design, slice, print, finish and cost 3D-printed parts safely and sell them honestly.
outcomes: Prepare a model and slice it.
Print and finish a useful part.
task: Design or select a part, print it, finish it, test it against a requirement and cost it for sale.
condition: Access to a printer (own, makerspace or partner), a computer, free software, two peers and a mentor.
standard: Part meets the dimensions within 0.3 mm; print log shows settings; failure analysis written; safety rules followed; cost per part shown; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Makers, students, product designers, small manufacturers.
evidence: model, slicer settings, print log, test record, cost sheet
modules: Pick the printer and material to match the part.
Filament printers melt plastic and lay it in layers; resin printers cure liquid with light.
PLA is easy and stiff; PETG is tougher; ABS resists heat but fumes need ventilation; resins give fine detail but need care.
Match material to heat, strength and food-contact needs.
Check local food-contact and safety rules before printing items for food.
A bracket for a shelf is printed in PETG for toughness; a jewellery prototype is printed in resin for detail. Most filament prints are not food safe without testing.
Compare four materials in a table. Add a food-contact note.
Table covers strength, heat and ease.
A model designed for printing prints well.
Wall thickness at least two nozzle widths.
Avoid steep overhangs or add supports.
Orientation affects strength; layers are weak in tension.
Allow tolerances of 0.2 to 0.4 mm for fits.
Print a tolerance test before fitting parts.
A bracket printed on its side is stronger because layer lines run along the load. A tolerance block shows 0.3 mm clearance works.
Design or choose a part and list its dimensions and orientation. Print or describe a tolerance test.

Layer height, infill, speed, temperature and supports.
Save slicer profiles for each material.
A part is sliced at 0.2 mm layers with 20 per cent infill and 3 walls, printing in 2.5 hours. A PETG profile prints at 235 degrees.
Slice your part and record settings. Save profiles.
Do not touch hot parts; keep hair and clothes clear.
Do not leave long prints unattended without safeguards.
Resin: gloves, eye protection and proper waste disposal.
A smoke alarm and a fire blanket are kept near the printer. A blanket is kept on the wall.
Print and log. Check safety kit.
Warping, stringing, poor adhesion and clogs.
Change one setting at a time.
Record each failure with a photo.
A heated bed and a brim fix warping on a large flat part. Photos show stringing at high temperature.
Use a respirator for sanding and spray paint.
Sanding progressively to 400 grit gives a smooth surface. A mask is worn for sanding.
Test three copies of the part.

ladder: Printers and materials

L1: learner can name printer types. Focus module: Printers and materials (Understand, 3 h). Pick the printer and material to match the part. Key points: Filament printers melt plastic and lay it in layers; resin printers cure liquid with light. PLA is easy and stiff; PETG is tougher; ABS resists heat but fumes need ventilation; resins give fine detail but need care. Match material to heat, strength and food-contact needs. Check manufacturer guidance. Check local food-contact and safety rules before printing items for food.

Teach: open with the worked example. A bracket for a shelf is printed in PETG for toughness; a jewellery prototype is printed in resin for detail. Most filament prints are not food safe without testing. Then set the activity: Compare four materials in a table. Add a food-contact note. Mark against the standard: Table covers strength, heat and ease. Check at this level: Easy filament? Model answer: PLA.
Design for printing

L2: learner knows safety. Focus module: Design for printing (Apply, 4 h). A model designed for printing prints well. Key points: Wall thickness at least two nozzle widths. Avoid steep overhangs or add supports. Orientation affects strength; layers are weak in tension. Allow tolerances of 0.2 to 0.4 mm for fits. Print a tolerance test before fitting parts.

Teach: open with the worked example. A bracket printed on its side is stronger because layer lines run along the load. A tolerance block shows 0.3 mm clearance works. Then set the activity: Design or choose a part and list its dimensions and orientation. Print or describe a tolerance test. Mark against the standard: Dimensions listed. Check at this level: Overhang fix? Model answer: Supports.
Slicing

L3: learner can slice. Focus module: Slicing (Apply, 4 h). The slicer turns a model into instructions. Key points: Layer height, infill, speed, temperature and supports. Preview the path before printing. Save profiles for materials. Check the first layer. Save slicer profiles for each material.

Teach: open with the worked example. A part is sliced at 0.2 mm layers with 20 per cent infill and 3 walls, printing in 2.5 hours. A PETG profile prints at 235 degrees. Then set the activity: Slice your part and record settings. Save profiles. Mark against the standard: Preview checked. Check at this level: Resin safety? Model answer: Gloves and eye protection.
Printing and safety

L4: learner can print. Focus module: Printing and safety (Apply, 4 h). Hot, moving and fumes. Key points: Ventilation and a stable surface. Do not touch hot parts; keep hair and clothes clear. Do not leave long prints unattended without safeguards. Resin: gloves, eye protection and proper waste disposal. Keep a fire blanket nearby.

Teach: open with the worked example. A smoke alarm and a fire blanket are kept near the printer. A blanket is kept on the wall. Then set the activity: Print and log. Check safety kit. Mark against the standard: Log complete. Check at this level: Why ventilate? Model answer: Fumes.
Troubleshooting

L5: learner can fix and cost. Focus module: Troubleshooting (Analyse, 3 h). Failures teach. Key points: Warping, stringing, poor adhesion and clogs. Change one setting at a time. Keep notes. Maintain the machine. Record each failure with a photo.

Teach: open with the worked example. A heated bed and a brim fix warping on a large flat part. Photos show stringing at high temperature. Then set the activity: Fix two issues. Photograph failures. Mark against the standard: Notes recorded. Check at this level: Warping fix? Model answer: Heated bed.
Testing the part

L6: learner can lead a lab. Focus module: Testing the part (Evaluate, 3 h). Does it meet the requirement? Key points: Dimension check with calipers. Load test within safe limits. Document the results. Retest after changes. Test three copies of the part.

Teach: open with the worked example. A bracket holds 5 kg for 10 minutes without deflection. Three copies hold 4.8, 5.1 and 5.0 kg. Then set the activity: Test and record. Test three copies. Mark against the standard: Record complete. Check at this level: Measuring tool? Model answer: Calipers.
Cost and sale

L7: learner can audit. Focus module: Cost and sale (Create, 3 h). Price honestly. Key points: Material, power, machine time, labour and failures. Quote per part. Disclose limits and intended use. Respect intellectual property. Include print time and failed print waste.

Teach: open with the worked example. Cost 62 INR; price 150 INR. A 10 per cent waste factor is applied. Then set the activity: Cost one part. Add waste. Mark against the standard: Currency shown. Check at this level: Costs? Model answer: Material, power, time, labour, failures.
